title: Equivalent fractions
text:
Two fractions are equivalent if we can recognize one of two relationships: 
 - $$ rac{a}{b}= rac{c}{d}$$ and $$ad=bc$$ 
 - $$ rac{b}{c}= rac{ab}{ac}$$ if a
eq $$0$$.

title: Example $$1$$
text: $$x+\frac{1}{x}$$ is not equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$. One way to see this is to plug in values. When $$x=2$$, $$x+\frac{1}{x}$$ is $$2.5$$, but $$\frac{x+1}{x}=1.5$$.

title: Example $$2$$
text: $$1-x$$ is not equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$. One way to see this is to plug in values. When $$x=1$$, $$1-x=0$$, but $$\frac{x+1}{x}=2$$.

title: Example $$3$$
text: $$\frac{x^2-1}{x^2-x}$$ is not equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$. Note that $$\frac{x^2-1}{x^2-x}=\frac{\left(x-1\right) \left(x+1\right)}{\left(x-1\right) x}$$. While this is of the form $$\frac{ab}{ac}$$, the issue here is that the multiple $$x-1$$ is not necessarily nonzero. So this expression is equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$ only when $$x-1$$ is not zero.

title: Example $$4$$
text: $$\frac{2\left(x+1\right)}{2x}$$ is equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$ since the numerator and denominator are both multiplied by the nonzero constant $$2$$.
